messages.author: 4fc972a92e1cec0a
messages.subject: Sampling weights in occu model
parts:
Hiya, 

I'm wondering whether there is a way to include weights in a simple occupancy model, for example when sampling density is uneven. I haven't found an example of this and I'm not sure whether it's just not implemented, or whether there are good reasons why this isn't usually carried out, or if I've missed a description of it somewhere in the documentation or papers (maybe I have the wrong search terms?). If it's just not implemented, I was thinking about adapting the code to add in weights to the likelihood. Hoping someone will let me know if this is a bad plan. 

Thanks, 
ali

messages.author: 3d5c753ab9984eeb
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Sampling weights in occu model
parts:
Hi

Sounds like you need an analog of detector-specific usage ('effort') in spatially explicit capture-recapture (but surprisingly missing from conventional capture-recapture). The idea there is to scale expected detection probability by known effort. This is exactly equivalent to an offset in regression - defined as a covariate whose coefficient is known in advance and therefore does not need to be estimated. Of course you can estimate the coefficient of the effort covariate if you like, it's just less elegant and marginally less efficient. We talked about this in MEE (2013) 4:629-636.

Murray

messages.author: 4fc972a92e1cec0a
messages.subject: Re: Sampling weights in occu model
parts:
Hey, 

 

Thanks Andy & Murray for the responses. [Delayed reply due to holiday last week]

 

I think this isn't an issue of variable effort, which describes the effort in a given site/time/sample. I can see this could be added as a covariate or an offset-style fixed parameter. However, here I’m talking about certain habitats (for example) having a greater number of samples (relative to their size). This could be a problem if different habitats have different effects of an environmental covariate or different occupancy trends, then the estimated coefficients would be dominated by the effect in the habitat with more samples. 

 

In a GLM the weightings to sort this out would be the inverse of the sampling density. For example, if there were two habitats which each cover 50% of the landscape, habitat A has data from 300 sites and habitat B has data from 100 sites. The sampling weights for the data points from habitat A would be 1/300 and for habitat B would be 1/100. The weights are used to multiply each data point in the likelihood, so that the contribution of each habitat to the likelihood ends up being 50%. The subsequent estimated coefficients should then be the correct balance of the coefficients in the two habitats, rather than dominated by habitat A effects in an unweighted version. I think this is distinct from variable effort, but maybe I’ve misunderstood your comments (Murray) and you’re referring to somehow using effort covariates to describe the sampling intensity?

 

I thought it might be quite straightforward to add a weighting term into the occu likelihood. I can try this with some simulations to see if it returns the expected result. I was surprised not to find any examples in the literature, although searches for “weight” were a bit dominated by AIC weights and similar, so there might be something out there that I missed. 

 

ali

messages.author: 3d5c753ab9984eeb
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Re: Sampling weights in occu model
parts:
Ali

Probably my comments on variable effort were a distraction... I'll try again. You describe a stratified sampling scenario. Classical methods for stratified sampling tell you how to combine stratum-specific estimates using the known stratum weights to get an overall estimate (Cochran 1977, Thompson 2002). We need to do this for e.g. patch-specific density estimates when sampling intensity varies among patches. I don't know whether this applies also  to coefficients of the model, but I don't see why not. My stats knowledge doesn't extend to whether you can embed the stratum weights in the likelihood (I understand a desire to avoid doing statistics on statistics, but maybe it is the more obvious route here).

Murray

messages.author: 4fc972a92e1cec0a
messages.subject: Re: Sampling weights in occu model
parts:
There are some examples of a post-hoc weighted average of different strata, eg. van Strien et al 2013. But ideally, I want to include the weights in the model, particularly as I have quite a messy stratification. 

I've had a go at adding weights to the likelihood with some simulations and it gives the result I expect. Estimates from a model with equal weights are equivalent to a naive average of the samples (both occupancy rate and environmental coefficients). Estimates from a model with sampling-intensity as weights are equivalent to a weighted average of the samples. So I think this is working ok. I've tested with a simple stratification and differences in occupancy or differences in the effect of a single covariate. The results are good for both. I realise the occupancy example is trivial as you would in reality include strata/habitat as a covariate, but I used it as a simple test example here. 

I'm happy to contribute the code if that would be helpful. But given I've not seen this approach documented for occupancy models, it would benefit from some more robust testing. I've only altered the R optimiser, not the C version. But I don't think it would be hard to add to both.

messages.author: 247b990d236a7af6
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Re: Sampling weights in occu model
parts:
I'm still not following from what you say as to how a combination (linear or otherwise) of estimated parameters won't get you what you want (with no special "weighting" involved in the estimation of the parameters).  Even with a messy stratification there needs to be specificity as to what you want in terms of the weights and the true parameters.

I'd also argue that what you need can't be justified by looking at the results.  I say this from your sentence "I've tested with a simple stratification and differences in occupancy or differences in the effect of a single covariate."  This almost sounds like the criterion is "I'll know it when I see it."

I'm not at all attempting to say that what you want is wrong.  I'm simply stating that I'm not seeing the specificity of the objective that would then guide one to modify a likelihood.  (But I've been very wrong before and as a statistician we're allowed to be wrong 5% of the time.)

Jim
